questions.title: Packages & Access Modifiers practice 1
questions.prompt: Which modifier limits a field to its own class?
choices: private
public
package
import
questions.explanation: A private member can be accessed only inside the class that declares it. Callers must use the public operations the class provides.

questions.title: Packages & Access Modifiers practice 2
questions.prompt: Which line imports ArrayList from its package?
choices: import java.util.ArrayList;
package java.util.ArrayList;
include java.util.ArrayList;
using java.util.ArrayList;
questions.explanation: Java import statements begin with `import` and use the full package and class name. The statement ends with a semicolon.

questions.title: Packages & Access Modifiers summary
questions.prompt: Which statement is accurate about Packages & Access Modifiers?
choices: Organize classes and control which code may use their details.
It is used only to print a message.
It automatically fixes every program error.
It removes the need for variables and tests.
questions.explanation: A package groups related classes and gives them a shared name. Put the package statement first in the file. Use `public` for code meant for callers, `private` for class details, and default access for code shared only inside the package.

questions.title: Packages & Access Modifiers practice 5
questions.prompt: What does making `credits` private and exposing `addCredits` prevent?
choices: Outside code setting credits directly to an invalid value like -5
The class from being used in other packages
The credits field from ever changing
The object from being created
questions.explanation: A private field cannot be written from outside, so no caller can do `obj.credits = -5`. Changes must go through `addCredits`, which rejects a non-positive amount. The field still changes through that method, and the class is still usable elsewhere and still constructible.

questions.title: Package path match
questions.prompt: What should match `package school.records;` during a normal Java build?
choices: Keep the file under `school/records`. The declared package and folder path should match in normal builds.
Put a package declaration that does not match the folder path.
Make every field public for convenience.
Expose large public methods that do several unrelated jobs.
questions.explanation: The source path should mirror the package name, usually `school/records`. When the declaration and folder structure drift apart, imports and class loading become harder for both tools and humans to reason about.

questions.title: Package grouping
questions.prompt: How should classes be grouped into packages?
choices: Repeat full package names everywhere instead of importing.
Group classes that solve related problems.
Use default access when outside packages must call the member.
Hide a class that callers are supposed to construct.
questions.explanation: A package should gather classes that solve related problems. That keeps imports meaningful and helps students find where a type belongs instead of dropping every class into one crowded folder.

questions.title: Package declaration placement
questions.prompt: What should a review check when a Java file declares a package?
choices: Mix unrelated classes in one package.
Put the package statement after imports.
Match package names to the directory structure.
Use private access for methods other classes must call.
questions.explanation: The package declaration belongs at the top of the file and should match the directory layout used by the project. A mismatch often causes confusing import or compile behavior before the logic is even tested.

questions.title: Private fields
questions.prompt: Why keep fields private unless outside code truly needs direct access?
choices: Let package structure drift from the project structure.
Treat access modifiers as comments rather than compiler rules.
Expose implementation details as the public API.
Keep fields private unless outside access is truly required.
questions.explanation: Private fields let the class protect its own rules. Public methods can validate changes, preserve invariants, and expose only the operations callers are meant to use.

questions.title: Small public API
questions.prompt: What makes a public method easier for other classes to depend on?
choices: Expose small public methods with clear jobs.
Use one package for the entire application forever.
Import a class from the wrong package with the same name.
Make helper methods public only for tests without a reason.
questions.explanation: A public method should have a clear, stable job because outside callers may rely on it. Small public methods are easier to document and safer to keep compatible than broad methods with many hidden responsibilities.

questions.title: Imports versus long names
questions.prompt: Why import a class instead of repeating its full package name throughout a file?
choices: Forget that default access means package-private.
Import classes instead of repeating long names throughout a file.
Use package names that start with capital letters.
Change public method names without considering callers.
questions.explanation: Imports keep code readable while still making dependencies explicit at the top of the file. Repeating long fully qualified names clutters the logic and makes simple statements harder to scan.
